### Observed differences

- **Work is distributed across different resources in the later window.** In the earlier window, assignments in A01, A03, A13 / A14, A17 and A22 were each dominated by a group of resources led by User_65, who held roughly 8–13% of each activity's assignments, with several further resources at about 4–7% each. In the later window, User_65 and most of that group no longer appear among the ten most frequent assignees of any of these activities, while User_69 has become the largest assignee for all of them (about 10–15%) and User_18, together with several previously marginal resources, now holds about 4–7% each. The pooled share of the long tail of other resources fell only modestly, by roughly 3–5 percentage points per activity. Profile dissimilarity is 0.45–0.71, and every one of these differences is larger than in all but about 1 in 2,000 random re-splits. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]
- **Elapsed times between consecutive completions shortened.** The time from an A04 completion to the next A01 completion fell from a median of about 28 hours to about 19.5 hours (mean about 34 to about 22 hours), and the distribution tightened: the upper quartile dropped from about 45 to about 25 hours and the spread roughly halved, while the shortest quarter lengthened from almost 0 to about 2.6 hours. This rests on 200 intervals in each window. [TWAIT001]
- The elapsed time from A09 to the next A23 completion also shortened sharply (median from about 11 hours to about 1.3 hours), and the number of such consecutive pairs rose from 17 to 27; with only 17 and 27 intervals behind it, this observation is weakly supported. [TWAIT002]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the hypothesis that the allocation of work across resources changed: in the earlier window the six offer-handling activities (A01, A03, A13, A14, A17, A22) were dominated by a group of resources led by User_65, and in the later window a different group, led by User_69 together with User_18 and several others, took over comparable shares in every one of these activities. Supporting signs: the resource family produced 6 qualifying items against roughly 0.005 expected without change and the time family 2 against roughly 0.016, both many times the chance expectation, while the control-flow family produced none (0 against about 0.18), so the detected signal concerns allocation and timing rather than structure; all six assignment profiles moved in the same direction, with the same resources gaining and losing across activities, and every difference exceeds all but about 1 in 2,000 random re-splits. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, TWAIT001, TWAIT002]

Limitations: the six assignment items are not independent confirmations — A13 and A14 show identical profiles, and all six plausibly reflect one underlying reallocation — and the evidence cannot rule out that the two windows simply contain a different mix of cases rather than a change in how the same work is allocated; the resource codes are anonymous, so no roles can be attached to the gaining and losing groups. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]

Other differences: a consistent timing change stands beside the reallocation — intervals between consecutive completions of A04 and A01 shortened by roughly a third at the median with a much tighter spread, based on 200 intervals per window [TWAIT001], and intervals from A09 to A23 shortened from a median of about 11 to about 1.3 hours while their count rose from 17 to 27, though this rests on few intervals [TWAIT002]. Because these times measure elapsed time between consecutive completion events, the shortening could reflect faster handling or a different scheduling of the same work, and the evidence does not link it to the reallocation. [TWAIT001, TWAIT002]
